topic.title: Circle theorems: using them with reasons (proofs excluded)
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: One circle-theorem question in every M4 paper from 2018 to 2026, always in the last third: Q15–Q21 of the 19–26 questions on the paper, 3–9 marks with a median of 6 (Summer 2023 Q17 6 marks, Summer 2024 Q19 6, November 2024 Q15 6, Summer 2025 Q17 5, November 2025 Q20 6, Summer 2026 Q18 7). Part splits are [2, 2, 2], [1, 1, 4], [2, 3] or [1, 1, 5]: two or three short 'angle = ___° because ___' parts, then one unscaffolded part of 2–5 marks. Circle theorems also reappear in M8 alongside the equation of a circle.
mustMemorise: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, when both stand on the same arc
Angles in the same segment are equal (same side of the chord); on opposite sides they add up to 180°
The angle in a semicircle is 90°
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180° — never 'are equal'
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact
Two tangents from the same point outside the circle are equal, so the triangle they make with the chord is isosceles
Alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment, across the chord
A perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord, so r² = a² + d² with a half the chord
Every angle you write gets a theorem in full words on the same line; a reason attached to a wrong angle earns nothing

mustBeAbleTo: Quote all eight theorems in the words the scheme accepts, and write one on the same line as every angle you find

Use opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral after checking that all four vertices are on the circle

sheet.howExamined: M4 (calculator, 2 hours, 100 marks). One circle-theorem question in every paper since 2018, placed at Q15–Q21, always in the last third, and worth 3–9 marks, most often 6 (Summer 2023 Q17, Summer 2024 Q19, November 2024 Q15, Summer 2025 Q17, November 2025 Q20, Summer 2026 Q18). The layout is 'Angle ___ = ______ ° because ____________', two or three times, then one unscaffolded part of 2–5 marks: a two-step chain, an algebraic angle, or an 'explain why' that refutes a claim. Schemes award A1 for the angle and MA1 for the reason, so a wrong angle costs both; an explanation part is usually MA2 for the whole argument.
traps: Reasons that leave out a required word — 'opposite', 'cyclic', 'alternate segment' — score nothing even when the angle is right (November 2025 M4 Q20)
'The angle is double' as the reason for the angle at the centre: it never says which angle (November 2025 M4 Q20)
'Z angles' or 'alternate angles' for two angles in the same segment: there are no parallel lines in a circle diagram (November 2025 M4 Q20)
Claiming that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are equal (Summer 2025 M4 Q17)
Treating two angles as opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral when one vertex is outside the circle (Summer 2024 M4 Q19)
Writing 'isosceles triangle' without saying that the two tangents from the point are equal (November 2024 M4 Q15)
Leaving the unscaffolded reasoning part blank, or giving angles with no reasons at all (Summer 2023 M4 Q17)
Refuting a diameter with 'it does not pass through the centre' instead of the angle in a semicircle (November 2025 M4 Q20)
Finding half a chord with Pythagoras and forgetting to double it
Not drawing the chord that turns two tangents into an isosceles triangle (Summer 2024 M4 Q19)

noteBlocks.lede: A circle has no corners, yet it pins angles down. Choose two points on the rim: every point on the same arc sees them at the same angle. Seven facts like that are the whole topic, and each one has a name you have to write out, the way you already name angles in a triangle.
can: Quote each theorem in the words the scheme accepts.
Name the theorem on the same line as every angle you find.
Tell the same segment from the opposite segment.

noteBlocks.md: Fix two points on the rim of a circle and join them to a third point somewhere on the major arc. Slide that third point anywhere along the arc and the angle it makes does not budge. Seven facts of that kind are the whole topic, and every one of them has a name the scheme insists on, exactly as you already write that angles in a triangle add to $180°$.

noteBlocks.prompt: The angles round the centre of a circle add up to how many degrees?
noteBlocks.explain: Angles at a point add up to 360°. That fact does the closing arithmetic in several of the chains below.

noteBlocks.md:
**The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference**, when both stand on the same arc. Learn it in those words, because a reason has to name both angles. The half-sentence *the angle is double* never says which angle is double which, so it does not earn the reason mark.
The centre angle is always the bigger one, so you divide going inwards and multiply going outwards. If the point at the circumference is on the **other** arc, the centre angle it stands on is the reflex one: $360 - 140 = 220$, and $220 \div 2 = 110$.

noteBlocks.prompt: The angle at the centre is 216°. The angle at the circumference standing on the same arc is
noteBlocks.explain: 216 ÷ 2. The centre angle is the larger, so the circumference angle is the half.

noteBlocks.md:
**Angles in the same segment are equal.** The segment is the region on one side of the chord, so P and Q have to be on the same arc.
Do not write *Z angles* or *alternate angles*. Those are parallel-line reasons and there are no parallel lines in a circle diagram; the reason mark is lost even when the angle is right. Cross the chord to R and the angles are no longer equal: APBR is a cyclic quadrilateral, so $60 + 120 = 180$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two points on the same arc give equal angles on a chord. Which reason is accepted?
options: Angles in the same segment are equal
They are Z angles
Angles in a circle are equal
noteBlocks.answer: Angles in the same segment are equal
noteBlocks.explain: The second is a parallel-line reason; the third is not a theorem at all.

noteBlocks.md:
**The angle in a semicircle is 90°.** It is the angle-at-the-centre theorem with a straight angle at the centre: $180 \div 2 = 90$.
The trigger is a chord that passes through the centre. Mark the right angle on the diagram before you write anything, and the rest of the triangle follows from $a + b = 90$. This theorem is also the one that settles the question *is this chord a diameter?*, which is where it turns up at the hard end of the paper.

noteBlocks.md:
**Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.** All four vertices must be on the circle: check that before you use it.
The reason has to carry three things — **opposite**, **cyclic quadrilateral**, and **180** — because *they add up to 180* on its own also describes angles on a straight line. Never write that they are equal; that is only true when both are 90°.

noteBlocks.title: Why opposite angles add to 180°
noteBlocks.md: Join both vertices to the centre. The two angles there go all the way round, so they add to $360°$. Each angle of the quadrilateral is half its own centre angle, so the pair adds to half of $360°$.

noteBlocks.prompt: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral and angle BAD = 131°. Angle BCD =
noteBlocks.explain: 180 − 131. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.

noteBlocks.md:
**A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact**, and **two tangents drawn from the same point outside a circle are equal**.
The second one is what makes triangle PAB isosceles, and it has to be said before the word isosceles: 'PA = PB, because two tangents from the same point are equal'. The kite OAPB gives the angle at the centre in one line, since $90 + 90 + \text{angle } APB + \text{angle } AOB = 360$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Complete the reason: triangle PAB is isosceles because two ______ from the same point outside the circle are equal.
noteBlocks.explain: PA and PB are the two tangent lengths, so they are equal and the base angles of triangle PAB are equal.

noteBlocks.md:
**The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment.** Alternate means *across the chord*: look at which side of the chord your tangent angle is on, then take the angle subtended from the other side.
Two checks that stop the common slips. The tangent-to-chord angle is not 90° — that is the tangent-to-**radius** angle. And the two angles at T add to 180°, so the two segments give $x$ and $180 - x$: pick the one across the chord.

noteBlocks.explain: They are equal. The angle in the other segment would be 180 − 47 = 133.

noteBlocks.md:
**A perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.** That single fact turns the picture into a right-angled triangle with the radius as the hypotenuse, so $r^2 = a^2 + d^2$.
The step that gets dropped is the last one. Pythagoras gives $a$, which is only **half** the chord; the answer is $2a$. Going the other way, from a chord of $2a$, halve it first.

noteBlocks.prompt: A chord is 8 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 17 cm. Its length, in cm, is
noteBlocks.explain: Half the chord is √(17² − 8²) = √225 = 15, and the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so the chord is 30 cm.

noteBlocks.text: Two-step chains: find the hidden isosceles triangle

noteBlocks.md:
The last part of a circle-theorem question rarely gives you a theorem to apply directly. It gives you a diagram with a triangle missing, and the triangle is always isosceles for one of two reasons: **two radii are equal**, or **two tangents from a point are equal**.
So the move is: draw the chord or the radius that creates that triangle, name why its two sides are equal, transfer an angle across with the alternate segment theorem, then use the angle sum of the triangle.

noteBlocks.prompt: PA and PB are tangents, C is on the major arc, and nothing joins A to B. What is your first line?
options: Join A to B, then PA = PB because two tangents from a point are equal
ACBP is a cyclic quadrilateral, so the two angles add to 180
Angle APB is at the centre, so halve it
noteBlocks.answer: Join A to B, then PA = PB because two tangents from a point are equal
noteBlocks.explain: P is outside the circle, so ACBP is not cyclic and P is certainly not the centre.

noteBlocks.md:
'Explain why this chord is not a diameter' is worth two marks and is answered in three short lines: **what a theorem would force**, **what the diagram actually gives**, **the conclusion**.
Take K, L, M and N on a circle, with angle NKL = 78°. If the chord LN were a diameter then the angle it subtends at the circumference would be 90°, because the angle in a semicircle is 90°. Angle NKL is 78°. So LN is not a diameter. Saying that LN 'does not pass through the centre' restates what a diameter is and scores nothing.

noteBlocks.prompt: A, B, C, D lie on a circle and angle ABC = 84°. Which line starts a two-mark explanation that AC is not a diameter?
options: If AC were a diameter, angle ABC would be 90°
AC is not the longest chord in the circle
The diagram shows AC missing the centre
noteBlocks.answer: If AC were a diameter, angle ABC would be 90°
noteBlocks.explain: The diagram is not drawn accurately and no lengths are given, so only the theorem can settle it.

noteBlocks.title: Sheet or memory?
noteBlocks.md:
**On the Higher formula sheet:** nothing for this topic.
**Must be known, in these words:** the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference; angles in the same segment are equal; the angle in a semicircle is 90°; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°; a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact; two tangents from the same point outside the circle are equal; the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment; the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.

Name the seven theorems in the words a marker can tick.
Double or halve between centre and circumference on the same arc.
Use a right angle wherever a chord passes through the centre.
Take opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral to $180°$.
Find the isosceles triangle made by two radii or two tangents.

One circle-theorem question in every paper, always in the last third. Every angle mark is paired with a reason mark, so name the theorem beside the angle on the same line. The last part is usually unscaffolded reasoning. Stuck: mark every angle you can and name the theorem that gave it.

noteBlocks.title: Not on this spec
noteBlocks.md: **Proofs of the circle theorems are excluded** by the Teacher Guidance on M4-GM-02. You are never asked to prove that the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference; you are asked to use it and to name it. Also outside this statement: the equation of a circle and the equation of a tangent (those are M8), and any theorem about intersecting chords or the alternate segment of a secant.

workedExamples.stem:
P, Q, R and S lie on a circle, centre O, in that order. Angle POR = 146°, measured on the side of O towards S.

Work out angle PQR and angle PSR. Give a reason for each answer.

figure.alt: Circle, centre O. P, Q, R and S lie on the circumference in that order, Q above O and S below it. OP and OR are radii with single tick marks. The angle POR at the centre, on the side towards S, is marked 146 degrees. The angle PQR and the angle PSR are each marked with an arc but no value.

steps.working: Angle POR and angle PQR both stand on the arc PR that does not contain Q.
steps.decision: Before any arithmetic, name the two angles: one is at the centre, one is at the circumference, and they stand on the same arc. That sentence is what turns the picture into a theorem.

steps.working: Angle PQR = 146 ÷ 2 = 73°, because the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.
steps.decision: Divide, because the centre angle is the big one. The reason is written in full: naming the centre and the circumference is what the scheme ticks.

options: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
The angle is double
The angles in a circle add up to 360°
whyMenu.explain: The second reason never says which angle is double which, so a marker cannot award it; the third is a different fact about angles at a point.

steps.working: P, Q, R and S lie on the circle in order, so PQRS is a cyclic quadrilateral. Angle PQR and angle PSR are opposite angles.
steps.decision: The second angle needs a different theorem, so first check that the four points really do form a cyclic quadrilateral and that the two angles really are opposite ones.

steps.working: Angle PSR = 180 − 73 = 107°, because opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.
steps.decision: Subtract from 180, not from 90, and not nothing at all. The words 'opposite' and 'cyclic' both have to be there.

options: They add up to 180°, so 180 − 73 = 107
They are equal, so angle PSR = 73°
The angle at the centre is doubled, so angle PSR = 146°
whyMenu.explain: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, not equal. Summer 2025 M4 Q17 records candidates writing that they are equal and losing the reason mark.

steps.working: Check: the reflex angle POR is 360 − 146 = 214°, and 214 ÷ 2 = 107°, which agrees with angle PSR.
steps.decision: S is on the other arc, so the angle at the centre it stands on is the reflex one. The check costs ten seconds and catches a 73 written where 107 belongs.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Angle PQR = 73° (the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference); angle PSR = 107° (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°).

workedExamples.stem:
A and B lie on a circle. PA and PB are tangents to the circle, and C is a point on the major arc AB. Angle ACB = 5y° and angle APB = 2y°.

Work out the value of y. Show each step of your working clearly.

figure.alt: Circle with A on the upper left and B on the lower left of the tangent point pair. PA and PB are tangents from the point P on the right, each marked with two tick marks to show they are equal. The chord AB is drawn as a dashed construction line. C is on the major arc, to the left. The angle ACB is marked 5y degrees and the angle APB is marked 2y degrees.

steps.working: Join A to B.
steps.decision: Nothing in the figure connects the two tangent points, so there is no triangle to work in. Drawing the chord AB is the whole question: Summer 2024 M4 Q19(c) was finished by 6% of candidates, and the ones who finished it drew this line.

steps.working: PA = PB, because two tangents from the same point are equal in length. So triangle PAB is isosceles and angle PAB = angle PBA.
steps.decision: Say why the triangle is isosceles. November 2024 M4 Q15: 'isosceles triangle' on its own was not enough, because the equal sides had not been justified.

options: Two tangents from the same point outside the circle are equal
The triangle looks isosceles in the diagram
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius
whyMenu.explain: The diagram is not drawn accurately, so it proves nothing; the tangent-radius fact is true here but says nothing about the lengths PA and PB.

steps.working: Angle PAB = angle ACB = 5y°, by the alternate segment theorem (the angle between tangent PA and chord AB equals the angle in the alternate segment). In the same way angle PBA = 5y°.
steps.decision: Each base angle is the angle between a tangent and the chord AB, so each one equals the angle C in the alternate segment. Using the theorem twice is what makes the two base angles known.

steps.working: In triangle PAB: 2y + 5y + 5y = 180, so 12y = 180.
steps.decision: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. Writing the equation on its own line separates the geometry from the algebra.
Then angle APB = 30° and angle ACB = 75°.

steps.working: Check with the other route: angle OAP = angle OBP = 90° (a tangent is perpendicular to the radius), so angle AOB = 360 − 90 − 90 − 30 = 150°, and 150 ÷ 2 = 75° = angle ACB.
steps.decision: The tangent-kite route gives the same answer, so the value of y is safe. Either route earns the marks; this one is quicker if you have already drawn the radii.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: y = 15, so angle APB = 30° and angle ACB = 75°.

twin.stem: A and B lie on a circle, PA and PB are tangents, and C is on the major arc AB. Angle ACB = 4k° and angle APB = k°. Work out the value of k.

workedExamples.stem:
AB is a diameter of a circle, centre O, and C lies on the circle. BT is a tangent, touching the circle at B. Angle CAB = (2x + 5)° and angle ABC = (3x − 20)°.

Work out the value of x, then work out angle CBT, giving a reason for each step.

figure.alt: Circle, centre O. AB is a horizontal diameter with A on the left and B on the right; AO and OB carry single tick marks. C is on the circumference above, and the angle ACB is marked with a small square to show a right angle. The tangent BT runs vertically upwards from B, with a small square at B between BA and BT. The angle CAB is marked (2x + 5) degrees, the angle ABC is marked (3x - 20) degrees and the angle CBT is marked y degrees.

steps.working: Angle ACB = 90°, because the angle in a semicircle is 90°.
steps.decision: AB passes through O, so it is a diameter, and C is on the circumference: that is the semicircle theorem. Marking the right angle on the diagram before writing anything else keeps the next line honest.
The three angles of triangle ABC add up to 180°. Put the 90 in as a number, not as a picture.
Collect the x terms and the constants separately. The 90 moves across as −90 on the other side, which is why 105 and not 75 appears.

whyMenu.explain: The right angle is one of the three angles of the triangle, so it belongs on the left-hand side with the other two.

steps.decision: Substituting back is the fastest check there is, and it takes one line.

steps.working: Angle ABT = 90°, because a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. So angle CBT = 90 − 43 = 47°.
steps.decision: OB lies along AB, so the tangent at B is perpendicular to AB itself. Then angle CBT is what is left of the right angle after angle ABC is taken out.

steps.working: Check by the alternate segment theorem: the angle between tangent BT and chord BC equals the angle in the alternate segment, which is angle CAB = 47°.
steps.decision: Two different theorems give 47°, so the answer is safe. Either reason would be accepted, and quoting the alternate segment theorem is one line shorter.

twin.stem: AB is a diameter of a circle and C lies on the circle. Angle CAB = (3x − 4)° and angle ABC = (2x + 4)°. Work out the value of x.

workedExamples.stem:
A circle has centre O. A and B lie on it, and AB is a chord of length 9.6 cm. M is the point on AB for which OM is perpendicular to AB. C is a point on the major arc AB. Angle OAB = 34°.

Work out angle ACB and the length of AM, giving a reason for each step.

figure.alt: Circle, centre O. The chord AB is horizontal below O and is labelled 9.6 cm. The radii OA and OB are dashed and carry single tick marks. M is the midpoint of AB; OM is drawn vertically with a small square at M to show the right angle, and AM and MB each carry two tick marks. C is on the major arc above, joined to A and to B. The angle OAB is marked 34 degrees.

steps.working: OA = OB, because they are radii of the same circle. So triangle OAB is isosceles and angle OBA = angle OAB = 34°.
steps.decision: This is the hidden isosceles triangle the examiners keep writing about. It appears whenever two radii are drawn, and it has to be said out loud: 'OA and OB are radii, so they are equal'.

steps.working: Angle AOB = 180 − 34 − 34 = 112°, because the angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
steps.decision: Both base angles are 34°, so subtract twice. A single 34 here is the commonest slip in this chain.

steps.working: Angle ACB = 112 ÷ 2 = 56°, because the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.
steps.decision: Angle AOB is at the centre and angle ACB is at the circumference, and both stand on the arc AB that does not contain C, so the theorem applies.

options: Angle ACB = 56°, because the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
Angle ACB = 224°, because the angle at the circumference is twice the angle at the centre
Angle ACB = 112°, because angles in the same segment are equal
whyMenu.explain: The angle at the centre is always the larger of the two, so the circumference angle is the half, and C is not at the centre so the same-segment theorem does not connect it to angle AOB.

steps.working: AM = MB = 9.6 ÷ 2 = 4.8 cm, because the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
steps.decision: OM is stated to be perpendicular to AB and O is the centre, so M is the midpoint. The reason must name the perpendicular and the centre; 'M looks like the middle' earns nothing.

steps.working: Check: angle OAM = 34° and angle AMO = 90°, so angle AOM = 56°, which is half of angle AOB = 112°.
steps.decision: The perpendicular splits the isosceles triangle into two congruent right-angled triangles, so it halves the angle at the centre as well as the chord. The two halves agreeing is the check.

items.stem: A, B and C lie on a circle, centre O. Angle AOB = 130° and angle ACB = 65°. Which reason earns the mark?
items.skill: Write the angle-at-the-centre reason in the words the scheme accepts

figure.alt: Circle, centre O, with A and B on the circumference below O and C on the major arc above. The radii OA and OB carry single tick marks. The angle AOB is marked 130 degrees and the angle ACB is marked 65 degrees.

options.text: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.
options.feedback: This names both angles and says which is the larger. That is the wording the scheme ticks.
Double which angle, and where. The examiners record this half-sentence every series: the angle is right, the reason mark is not awarded because a marker cannot tell which angle is being doubled.

options.text: Angles in a circle add up to 360°.
options.feedback: That is a true fact about angles at a point, but it is not the theorem being used here and it does not connect 130 to 65.

items.stem: A, B, C and D lie in that order on a circle. Angle ABC = 84°. What is angle ADC?
items.skill: Apply the cyclic-quadrilateral theorem to opposite angles

options.feedback: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral and ABC and ADC are opposite angles, so they add up to 180°: 180 − 84 = 96.
Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°; they are only equal when both are 90°. Summer 2025 M4 Q17 records this exact claim from weaker candidates.
Halving belongs to the angle at the centre, and neither of these angles is at the centre. Both angles here are at the circumference.

items.stem: AB is a chord of a circle. P and Q are both on the major arc AB. Angle APB = 39°. What is angle AQB?
items.skill: Recognise two angles in the same segment

figure.alt: Circle with the chord AB drawn near the bottom. P and Q are both on the major arc above the chord and each is joined to A and to B. The angle APB is marked 39 degrees and the angle AQB is marked with a question mark.

options.feedback: P and Q are on the same arc, so angle APB and angle AQB are angles in the same segment and are equal.
That is the angle at a point on the other arc, where APBQ would be a cyclic quadrilateral and the two angles add to 180°. Here both points are on the same side of AB.
Doubling is the angle-at-the-centre theorem, and Q is on the circumference, not at the centre.

items.stem: Which angle in a circle diagram must be 90°?
items.skill: Separate the two right-angle theorems from the tangent-chord angle

options.text: The angle at the circumference standing on a diameter.
options.feedback: That is the angle in a semicircle. The other right angle in the list of theorems is the one between a tangent and the radius at the point of contact.

options.text: The angle between a tangent and a chord at the point of contact.
options.feedback: That angle equals the angle in the alternate segment and can be any size. It is 90° only when the chord happens to be a diameter.

options.text: The angle at the centre standing on a chord.
options.feedback: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so it is 90° only when the angle at the circumference is 45°.

items.stem: PA and PB are tangents drawn to a circle from the point P outside it, with AB joined. Which reason fully justifies the statement 'triangle PAB is isosceles'?
items.skill: Justify the isosceles triangle made by two tangents

options.text: Two tangents drawn from the same point outside a circle are equal, so PA = PB.
options.feedback: The equal sides are named and the theorem behind them is quoted. November 2024 M4 Q15 shows that this sentence is what the mark is for.

options.text: Triangle PAB is isosceles because the diagram is symmetrical.
options.feedback: Every circle-theorem diagram is printed with 'diagram not drawn accurately', so nothing can be read off it. The tangent theorem has to be quoted.

options.text: A tangent is perpendicular to the radius, so PA = PB.
options.feedback: That theorem is true in this diagram, but it is about angles at A and at B, not about the lengths PA and PB.

items.stem: STU is a tangent touching a circle at T, and TB is a chord. Angle BTU = 58°. Which other angle is 58°?

options.text: Angle TAB, where A is a point on the arc on the opposite side of TB from U.
options.feedback: The angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment: the segment on the other side of the chord.

options.text: Angle TCB, where C is a point on the arc on the same side of TB as U.
options.feedback: That is the angle in the other segment, so it is 180 − 58 = 122°. The word 'alternate' is the instruction to cross the chord.

options.text: The angle between the chord TB and the radius OT.
options.feedback: That angle is 90 − 58 = 32°, because the tangent and the radius meet at 90°. The alternate segment theorem never mentions the radius.

items.stem: A, B, C and D lie in that order on a circle and angle ABC = 84°. Which explanation shows that AC cannot be a diameter of the circle?
items.skill: Refute a claim with a theorem rather than with a description

options.text: If AC were a diameter then angle ABC would be 90°, because the angle in a semicircle is 90°. Angle ABC is 84°, so AC is not a diameter.
options.feedback: A theorem is quoted, a number is tested against it and the conclusion follows. November 2025 M4 Q20(c) was answered this way by the 6% who scored.

options.text: AC does not pass through the centre of the circle.
options.feedback: That restates what a diameter is, so it assumes the very thing being asked. A theorem has to do the work.

options.text: AC is not the longest chord in the circle, so it cannot be a diameter.
options.feedback: True of a diameter, but nothing in the question gives any lengths, so there is nothing to compare. The angle at B is the information you were given.

parts.stem:
A, B and C lie on a circle, centre O.
Angle AOB = 128°.

Work out the value of x, giving a reason for your answer.  [2]

Answer  x = ______ °  because ________________________________________

accepted: 64 because the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference

any: angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
angle at the centre is two times the angle at the circumference
angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference
the angle subtended at the centre is twice the angle subtended at the circumference

scheme.for: reason: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
accept: angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference
scheme.examinerNote: November 2025 M4 Q20: a wrong angle removed the credit for its reason, so the reason mark depends on the angle.

hints: Angle AOB is at the centre and angle ACB is at the circumference. Which of the two is the larger.
Both angles stand on the arc AB that does not contain C, so the theorem applies. Divide by 2.
Write the reason as a full sentence naming the centre and the circumference.
parts.workedSolution: Angle AOB is the angle at the centre and angle ACB is the angle at the circumference, both standing on the arc AB that does not contain C. So $x = 128 \div 2 = 64$. Reason: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.

commonErrors.feedback: The 64 earns the first mark. The reason mark needs both angles named: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference.
128 was doubled instead of halved. The angle at the centre is always the larger of the two, so the angle at the circumference is the half.

context.setting: Circle, centre O, with three points on the circumference

figures.alt: Circle, centre O. A and B are on the circumference below O and C is on the major arc above. The radii OA and OB carry single tick marks. The angle ACB is marked 37 degrees and the angle AOB is marked y degrees.

Angle ACB = 37°.

Work out the value of y.  [2]

Answer  y = ______ °

scheme.for: 2 × 37 seen, or the statement that the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference

hints: This time the unknown is the angle at the centre.
The angle at the centre is the larger one, so multiply rather than divide.
parts.workedSolution: Angle AOB is at the centre and angle ACB is at the circumference, both standing on arc AB. The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, so $y = 2 \times 37 = 74$.

commonErrors.feedback: 37 was halved. The angle at the centre is the larger of the two, so it is 2 × 37.
180 − 37 belongs to opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral. There is no quadrilateral here: O is the centre, not a point on the circumference.

Angle APB = 41°.

any: angles in the same segment are equal
angles in the same segment
same segment

hints: P and Q are on the same side of the chord AB.
Both angles stand on the same arc, so they are angles in the same segment.
parts.workedSolution: P and Q lie on the same arc, so angle APB and angle AQB are angles in the same segment and are equal. $x = 41$.

Fill in the right angle at C first, then use the angle sum of the triangle.

Angle DAB and angle BCD are opposite angles of that quadrilateral.

context.setting: Tangent from an external point with the radius drawn

figures.alt: Circle, centre O, with T on the circumference to the right of O. The radius OT is horizontal with a single tick mark. The tangent runs from T up to the point P outside the circle, and a small square at T marks the right angle between OT and TP. OP is drawn dashed. parts.stem:
O is the centre of a circle and T lies on the circle. PT is a tangent, touching the circle at T.
Angle TOP = 58°.

Work out the value of x.  [2]

Answer  x = ______ °

scheme.for: angle OTP = 90 used (a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact)

hints: OT is a radius and PT is a tangent touching the circle at T.
Mark the right angle at T, then use the angle sum of triangle OTP.
parts.workedSolution: PT is a tangent and OT is the radius drawn to the point of contact, so angle OTP = 90°. In triangle OTP the angles add up to 180°, so $x = 180 - 90 - 58 = 32$.

commonErrors.feedback: 180 − 58 treats OTP as a straight line. The right angle sits at T, between the radius and the tangent, and is one of the three angles of the triangle.
The triangle is not isosceles: OT is a radius and TP is a tangent, so there is no reason for two of its sides to be equal.

context.setting: Two tangents from an external point

figures.alt: Circle with A above and B below the tangent point pair. PA and PB are tangents from the point P on the right and each carries two tick marks to show they are equal. The chord AB is drawn. The angle APB is marked 46 degrees and the angle PAB is marked x degrees.

parts.stem:
A and B lie on a circle. PA and PB are tangents to the circle, and AB is joined.
Angle APB = 46°.

parts.stem:
O is the centre of a circle of radius 7.4 cm. AB is a chord, and M is the point on AB for which OM is perpendicular to AB. OM = 4.6 cm.

Calculate the length of AB.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.  [3]

Answer  AB = ______ cm

scheme.for: AB = 11.6 cm, the AM value doubled because the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord
scheme.examinerNote: AM alone, left undoubled, scores MA1 MA2 only.

hints: Triangle OMA has a right angle at M, with the radius OA as the hypotenuse.
M is the midpoint of AB, because the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. Double AM.
parts.workedSolution: Triangle OMA has a right angle at M and OA = 7.4 cm is the hypotenuse, so $AM = \sqrt{7.4^2 - 4.6^2} = \sqrt{33.6} = 5.7966$ cm. OM is perpendicular to the chord AB and O is the centre, so M is the midpoint of AB and $AB = 2 \times 5.7966 = 11.5931$, which is 11.6 cm to 3 significant figures.

commonErrors.feedback: Two of the three marks: the Pythagoras step is right, but AM is only half of AB. The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, so double it.
7.4 − 4.6 = 2.8 is not a length in this diagram, and doubling it is not AB. The 7.4 cm is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle, so Pythagoras is needed.

parts.stem:
C is a point on the major arc AB.

Work out angle ACB, giving a reason for each step of your working.
Give your answer to 1 decimal place.  [3]

Answer  angle ACB = ______ °

scheme.for: angle OAB found, e.g. sin(angle OAB) = 4.6 ÷ 7.4 giving 38.4°
angle AOB = 180 − 2 × 38.4 = 103.1°, with OA = OB because they are radii, so triangle OAB is isosceles
angle ACB = 51.6°, with the reason 'the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference'
scheme.examinerNote: Accept 51.6 or 51.57; a bare answer with no reasons scores this mark only.

hints: Start in the right-angled triangle OMA, where you know two sides.
OA and OB are radii, so triangle OAB is isosceles: both base angles are equal.
Angle AOB is at the centre and angle ACB is at the circumference, standing on the same arc.
parts.workedSolution: In triangle OMA, $\sin(\text{angle } OAB) = 4.6 \div 7.4$, so angle OAB = 38.43°. OA = OB because they are radii of the same circle, so triangle OAB is isosceles and angle OBA = angle OAB. The angles of the triangle add up to 180°, so angle AOB = $180 - 2 \times 38.43 = 103.13$°. Angle AOB is at the centre and angle ACB is at the circumference, both standing on the arc AB that does not contain C, so angle ACB = $103.13 \div 2 = 51.57$°, which is 51.6° to 1 decimal place. The shorter route gives the same value: OM bisects the isosceles triangle, so angle AOM = angle ACB, and $\cos(\text{angle } AOM) = 4.6 \div 7.4$ gives 51.6° in one step.

commonErrors.feedback: 103.1° is angle AOB, the angle at the centre. The angle at the circumference is half of it.
Only one base angle was subtracted, giving angle AOB = 141.6° instead of 103.1°. Triangle OAB is isosceles because OA and OB are radii, so both base angles are the same size.
Rounding angle OAB to 38° part-way through moves the final answer from 51.6° to 52.0°. Keep the calculator value in the working and round only on the answer line.

findTheMistake.stem: AB is a chord of a circle, with P and Q both on the major arc AB, and angle APB = 54°. Rhea was asked for angle AQB, giving a reason for her answer. Her answer:
studentWorking: AP and QB make a Z shape across the circle
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The angle is right and the shape she noticed is real, but 'Z angles' is the reason for alternate angles on parallel lines, and there are no parallel lines in the diagram. A circle-theorem question needs a circle theorem: angles in the same segment are equal.
correction: P and Q are both on the major arc AB, so they are in the same segment
because angles in the same segment are equal
findTheMistake.feedback: A1 for 54°. The reason mark is the one at risk, and it is the one the reports keep flagging: the words have to name the theorem. Write 'angles in the same segment are equal' and the second mark follows. November 2025 M4 Q20 records reasons that missed the required words and scored nothing.

findTheMistake.stem: A, B, C and D lie on a circle and angle BAD = 107°. Niamh was asked for angle BCD, giving a reason. Her answer:
studentWorking: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral must match
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is exactly right, and it is the hardest part. Line 2 states the theorem wrongly: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°, they are not equal. They are only equal in the special case when both are 90°.
correction: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing scores here, because the wrong theorem produced a wrong angle and a reason cannot rescue an angle that is wrong. Summer 2025 M4 Q17 names this exact claim from weaker candidates. A one-second check: if the two opposite angles were equal and one of them is obtuse, the other would be obtuse too, and four obtuse angles cannot add to 360°.

findTheMistake.stem: K, L, M and N lie on a circle, centre O, and angle NKL = 78°. Órlaith was asked to explain why the chord LN is not a diameter. Her answer, worth 2 marks:
studentWorking: LN does not pass through the centre of the circle
so LN is not a diameter
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 says what a diameter is, so it assumes the very point that was to be explained, and it reads the diagram, which is printed 'not drawn accurately'. A claim is refuted by testing it against a theorem, not by describing it.
correction: If LN were a diameter, then angle NKL would be 90°, because the angle in a semicircle is 90°
so LN is not a diameter
findTheMistake.feedback: Zero out of 2 as written. The structure that scores is three short lines: what the theorem would force, what the diagram actually gives, and the conclusion. Only 6% of candidates managed it in November 2025 M4 Q20(c), and this is the whole difference between them and everyone else.

prompts.prompt: The routine for any circle-theorem question with reasons.
prompts.answer: 1 Mark every angle you are given on the diagram. 2 Look for the standard shapes: a diameter, a cyclic quadrilateral, two radii, a tangent with a chord, two tangents from a point. 3 Write each new angle with its theorem in full words on the same line. 4 If nothing is joined up, draw the chord or radius that makes a triangle. 5 Check the total: angles in a triangle 180°, in a quadrilateral 360°.

prompts.prompt: Name all eight circle theorems on this specification.
prompts.answer: 1 The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference. 2 Angles in the same segment are equal. 3 The angle in a semicircle is 90°. 4 Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°. 5 A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. 6 Two tangents from the same point outside the circle are equal. 7 The alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord equals the angle in the alternate segment. 8 The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.

prompts.prompt: A candidate writes 'the angle is double' as the reason for halving an angle at the centre. What is missing, and what does it cost.
prompts.answer: The sentence never says which angle is double which. The accepted wording names both: the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference. The angle itself still scores, so the loss is one reason mark on a two-mark part.
keyWords: at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference

prompts.prompt: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are ______ . Which word must never appear here.
prompts.answer: They add up to 180°. The word that must never appear is 'equal'. The reason also has to keep the words 'opposite' and 'cyclic': 'they add to 180' on its own describes angles on a straight line as well.

prompts.prompt: Two angles stand on the same chord, from two points on the same arc. Why is 'Z angles' not an accepted reason.
prompts.answer: Z angles, or alternate angles, is a parallel-line reason, and a circle diagram has no parallel lines in it. The accepted wording is 'angles in the same segment are equal'. If the two points are on opposite arcs, the angles are not equal at all: they add up to 180° because the four points form a cyclic quadrilateral.
keyWords: angles in the same segment are equal

prompts.prompt: State the alternate segment theorem, and say how you find the alternate segment in a diagram.
prompts.answer: The angle between a tangent and a chord drawn from the point of contact equals the angle in the alternate segment. To find it, look at the side of the chord your angle is on, then cross the chord: the angle you want is subtended by that same chord from a point on the other side.

prompts.prompt: You have written 'triangle PAB is isosceles' for a triangle made by two tangents. What must be written before it.
prompts.answer: PA = PB, because two tangents from the same point are equal in length. Without that sentence the isosceles claim is unjustified and the mark is not awarded, which is what November 2024 M4 Q15 records.
keyWords: two tangents from the same point are equal

prompts.prompt: Where are the two guaranteed right angles in circle-theorem work, and which angle is often mistaken for one of them.
prompts.answer: The angle in a semicircle, at a point on the circumference standing on a diameter; and the angle between a tangent and the radius drawn to the point of contact. The angle between a tangent and a chord is not one of them: it equals the angle in the alternate segment and can be any size.

prompts.prompt: A chord of length 2a is drawn in a circle of radius r. The perpendicular from the centre meets it at M. What do you know, and what can you calculate.
prompts.answer: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord, so M is the midpoint and each half is a. Triangle OMA has a right angle at M with hypotenuse r, so the distance from the centre is √(r² − a²). Working the other way, if the distance d is known then a = √(r² − d²) and the chord is 2√(r² − d²): the doubling at the end is the step that gets left out.

prompts.prompt: A diagram gives two tangents from a point P touching at A and B, and an angle at a point C on the major arc. Nothing joins A to B. What is the first thing you do.
prompts.answer: Draw the chord AB. It turns the two tangents into the isosceles triangle PAB, and each base angle is then a tangent-to-chord angle, equal to the angle at C by the alternate segment theorem. Summer 2024 M4 Q19(c) was completed by 6% of candidates, and drawing that chord is what the successful answers did first.

prompts.prompt: A, B, C and D lie on a circle and angle ABC = 84°. Explain in two sentences why the chord AC is not a diameter.
prompts.answer: If AC were a diameter, angle ABC would be 90°, because the angle in a semicircle is 90°. Angle ABC is 84°, which is not 90°, so AC is not a diameter. Saying instead that AC 'does not pass through the centre' scores nothing: it restates the definition rather than using a theorem.

prompts.prompt: In this diagram STU is a tangent at T and A is on the circumference. Which theorem makes the two marked angles equal, and what would happen to the equality if A moved to the arc between T and B.
prompts.answer: The alternate segment theorem: the angle between the tangent TU and the chord TB equals the angle TAB in the alternate segment. If A moved to the short arc between T and B it would be in the other segment, and the angle there would be the supplement instead, 180° minus the marked angle.

findings.asked: Find two angles with circle theorems; then an open reasoning question.
findings.wentWrong: The angle-finding was very good. The reasoning part was mostly zero: left blank, or angles found with no reasons at all. One mark was available for starting with the alternate segment theorem.
findings.rule: In a reasoning question every angle you write must carry a theorem.

findings.asked: Angle at the centre; alternate segment; then find an angle expression in an unscaffolded configuration.
findings.wentWrong: Parts (a) and (b) were mostly fine, though the alternate segment theorem was less secure. In (c) only 6% finished: the common error was to treat two angles as opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Drew the chord joining the two contact points, used the alternate segment theorem twice to get two equal base angles, then used the angle sum of a triangle.
findings.rule: Add the chord that turns the tangents into an isosceles triangle.

findings.asked: A scaffolded circle-theorem chain with reasons.
findings.wentWrong: Angles were right but reasons wrong. In the last part 'isosceles triangle' was written without saying why: the two tangents from the external point are equal.
findings.rule: Two tangents from a point are equal - say so before saying 'isosceles'.

findings.asked: An angle with a reason; then a two-step angle.
findings.wentWrong: Most found the first angle but gave incomplete reasons; weaker candidates claimed opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are equal. Part (b) needed 'triangle BDE is isosceles' plus the alternate segment theorem; very few gave both.
findings.rule: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180 degrees; two-step questions need the isosceles triangle named.

findings.asked: Angles with reasons; then explain why a chord cannot be a diameter.
findings.wentWrong: Reasons omitted key words ('opposite', 'cyclic'); a wrong angle removed any credit for its reason. Only 6% could refute the diameter claim: 'it does not go through the centre' is not a theorem; the angle in a semicircle argument was wanted.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Showed the angle subtended by the chord was not 90 degrees, so the chord cannot be a diameter.
findings.rule: Refute with a theorem: a diameter subtends a right angle at the circumference.

insight.ruleToRemember: Every angle gets a theorem in exact words. Look for the hidden isosceles triangle (two radii, or two tangents from a point) and draw the chord that creates it; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180 degrees.
insight.aStarSignal: The unscaffolded 'explain why' - chaining alternate segment, isosceles and angle sum, or refuting a claim via the angle in a semicircle - with reasons a marker can tick.
